10-k.txt:1803: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
10-k.txt:1804: OVERVIEW
10-k.txt:1805: SUNation Energy, Inc. (herein referred to as “SUNation Energy,” “SUNE,” “our,” “we” or the “Company”) is focused on growing leading local and regional solar, storage, and energy services companies nationwide. The SUNation Energy vision is the provision of exemplary client service while powering the energy transition through grass-root, community-centric growth of solar electricity paired with battery storage. Our portfolio of brands (SUNation, Hawaii Energy Connection, E-Gear) provide homeowners and businesses of all sizes with an end-to-end product offering spanning solar, battery storage, and grid services. SUNation Energy, Inc.’s markets are New York and Hawaii, and the company operates proudly within two U.S. states.
10-k.txt:1806: Our primary customers are residential homeowners. We also provide solar energy systems to commercial owners and other municipal customers.
10-k.txt:1807: Corporate History
10-k.txt:1808: SUNation Energy is a Delaware corporation originally organized in 1969 that operates directly and through its subsidiaries located in the United States (“U.S.”).
10-k.txt:1809: SUNation Energy’s vision is to power the energy transition through grass-roots growth of solar electricity paired with battery storage. The Company is a domestic operator and consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services solutions. Our strategy is focused on acquiring, integrating, and growing leading local and regional solar, storage, and energy services companies nationwide.
10-k.txt:1810: Our current business units,
10-k.txt:1811: Hawaii Energy Connection, LLC (“HEC”), and New York-based subsidiaries, the SUNation entities (collectively, “SUNation NY”)
10-k.txt:1812: are engaged in the design, installation, and maintenance of solar energy systems across residential, commercial, and municipal sectors. Our team specializes in providing tailored solar solutions that meet the specific energy needs of each client, ensuring both efficiency and sustainability. In addition to our core solar services, we also offer energy storage systems to optimize energy use and increase reliability. Our New York business unit further integrates a broader range of services, including residential roofing solutions, to ensure seamless solar installations and long-term durability. Additionally, we provide community solar services that allow groups of individuals, businesses, or organizations to share the benefits of a single solar array, making renewable energy accessible to more people in the community.
10-k.txt:1813: Our Strategy
10-k.txt:1814: Our strategy is designed to provide customers with sustainable energy security by leveraging our people, technology, and processes to deliver solutions that improve the performance, increase the reliability, and reduce the cost of energy. Key elements of our strategy include:
10-k.txt:1815: 
10-k.txt:1816: Capitalizing on the opportunity for industry and regional consolidation.
10-k.txt:1817: Residential solar is a fragmented industry, with over 4,000 contractors nationwide. We believe the
10-k.txt:1818: Tesla-SolarCity acquisition in 2016 and the
10-k.txt:1819: Sunrun-Vivint merger in 2020 started an era of consolidation and the positive impact of scale-expansion. According to Wood Mackenzie, as of 2025 Q4, 75%+ of the residential solar market is served by a regional or local installer. We believe there is a tremendous opportunity for a consolidator to rapidly scale its business and become one of the most recognized brands in the industry through acquiring, integrating, and growing leading local and regional solar sales and installation companies.
10-k.txt:1820: 
10-k.txt:1821: Leverage and continue to lower our customer acquisition costs through referral programs.
10-k.txt:1822: We already have what we believe are premier referral rates, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers. We believe that our existing HEC and SUNation NY portfolio companies form a foundation to drive improved referral performance across the network of companies we acquire, further increasing our referral rates and lowering our overall customer acquisition cost.
10-k.txt:1823: 
10-k.txt:1824: Continue to grow our operations to achieve economies of scale.
10-k.txt:1825: Residential and Commercial solar is like many industries in that cost-of-goods-sold is a significant expense, and companies with greater scale can enjoy significantly lower costs throughout their equipment supply chain. As we grow both organically and through acquisitions, we expect to lower the costs of acquiring key input products such as modules, inverters, and electrical balance-of-systems components, which we anticipate should allow us to accelerate growth through lower pricing and enhanced profit margins. With scalable shared services (e.g., accounting, HR, policy, marketing, legal, IT), we believe our current approach of organic growth enhanced by acquisitions will drive profitability and cash generation. We are also able to help our customers access various options to finance their acquisition of a solar system through referrals to a variety of solar finance companies.
10-k.txt:1826: 
10-k.txt:1827: Explore potential opportunities outside of solar to become a one-stop shop for consumers’ home and energy needs.
10-k.txt:1828: As we continue to grow our customer base, we may have new opportunities for incremental revenue generation by cross-selling
10-k.txt:1829: 6
10-k.txt:1830: ancillary market products such as more energy storage and service contracts on orphaned systems (customers whose original solar contractor is no longer in business or have simply abandoned the local markets).
10-k.txt:1831: We believe that the following key strengths of our business position us to execute on our M&A roll-up strategy and to distinguish us from competitors.
10-k.txt:1832: 
10-k.txt:1833: Customer centric approach in market, leading to competitive customer acquisition costs.
10-k.txt:1834: SUNation Energy seeks to put the customer above all else. Our installers complete offerings in-house as full-service installers to have total control of the customer experience. Our Company offers transparent, clear sales agreements and has invested in digital tools to support customers along the installation journey. Our installers are active in their local communities to build a trusted brand. These activities lead to satisfied customers, as demonstrated by a high average referral rate and favorable online reviews, helping to lower future customer acquisition costs.
10-k.txt:1835: 
10-k.txt:1836: A leading vendor for cutting-edge product offerings.
10-k.txt:1837: We are a leading vendor for cutting-edge product offerings from Enphase, Tesla, FranklinWH, and other large solar product providers. As an experienced operator in the residential and commercial solar industries, we have built relationships with these large solar product providers.
10-k.txt:1838: In 2026, we will be expanding this product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem, which includes their new power electronics, whole home batteries, standby generators, and smart thermostat that control the entire system.
10-k.txt:1839: 
10-k.txt:1840: Seasoned and experienced management team.
10-k.txt:1841: We have a strong leadership team, with deep experience in residential and commercial solar and M&A. Our chief executive officer grew our New York business into the third largest solar provider in one of the most dynamic markets in the country. Our chief operating officer and chief financial officer is a seasoned leader in the M&A, finance, technology and solar markets. We have over 100 years of solar industry experience at the management level.
10-k.txt:1842: Our Products and Services
10-k.txt:1843: The primary product we offer to customers is a photovoltaic solar energy system, which is almost always installed on the roof, although can at times be ground mounted. Solar panels, also called modules, generate direct-current electricity when they are struck by sunlight. This direct current (“DC”) is sent to an inverter, which converts the DC electricity into alternating-current (“AC”) electricity, which is the type of electricity that is needed to provide power to outlets and run home appliances and equipment The AC flows from the inverter to the home’s main electrical panel, where it is then used to supply the home, business, or institution’s current power needs. If there is a shortfall, the home draws the remainder needed from the traditional utility connection, often referred to as the “grid.” If the home system has excess production, the surplus is usually exported back to the grid. Residential solar systems typically provide cost savings to customers because the system’s roof-panels generate power from the sun instead of customer’s needing to purchase power from the utility. In addition, customers generally receive tax incentives and credits for the excess generation provided back to the utility.
10-k.txt:1844: Battery storage is an increasingly important piece of our offering. Lithium-ion batteries store excess solar generated electricity on the residential premises, as opposed to sending it back to the grid. This can generate economic benefits in markets with utility time-of-use (“TOU”) rates, whereby a homeowner is compensated at a low rate during the day for sending solar to the grid but would be charged a high rate in the evening for drawing electricity from the grid. In TOU markets, customers can store their excess power during the day and then utilize the stored power at night, thus saving money. An equally important benefit of pairing a battery with solar is that a battery will keep powering a customer’s home during a grid outage. A solar system alone will not continue providing a home with electricity if the grid is down as the utility company establishes automatic disconnects to ensure that no live current is sent back into the grid for safety reasons. When a battery is added, the system can automatically and nearly-instantaneously become a self-contained micro-grid during an outage. The home can continue utilizing the electricity generated by the panels, as well as electricity stored in the battery when the sun is not shining. In addition, the excess production from the panels during the day can be used to recharge a battery that was depleted overnight.
10-k.txt:1845: In the Hawaiian market we also offer energy management control devices on solar systems that are paired with batteries that help homeowners generate ongoing revenue streams by aggregating their batteries into a fleet, thus creating a “virtual power plant” and selling grid services to the utility. We have proprietary technology in this area, and strong relationships with regulators and utilities.
10-k.txt:1846: Residential Customers Agreements
10-k.txt:1847: The majority of SUNation Energy’s revenue (85% of 2025 consolidated revenue) comes from photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries for residential homeowners. The size of our residential installations vary by location. In 2025, the average system size installed was 6.8 kilowatts for HEC customers in Hawaii and 127 kilowatts for SUNation NY’s regional customers on Long Island, New York.
10-k.txt:1848: Historically, most residential homeowners have chosen to own their home system rather than pursue a third-party ownership model. The Company believes that it has historically been best for customers to own their own systems, but recognizes that some customers do not want to own their systems.

10-k.txt:2349: The following discussion and analysis should be read in conjunction with the Company’s Consolidated Financial Statements and the related notes that appear elsewhere in this report.
10-k.txt:2350: Overview

Our team specializes in providing tailored solar solutions that meet the specific energy needs of each client, ensuring both efficiency and sustainability. In addition to our core solar services, we also offer energy storage systems to optimize energy use and increase reliability. Our New York business unit further integrates a broader range of services, including residential roofing solutions, to ensure seamless solar installations and long-term durability. 10-k.txt:2358: Reverse Stock Splits
10-k.txt:2359: June 2024 Reverse Stock Split
10-k.txt:2360: On January 3, 2024, the Company’s shareholders approved a reverse stock split of the Company’s common stock at a ratio within a range of 1-for-2 and 1-for-15 and granted the Company’s board of directors the discretion to determine the timing and ratio of the split within such range.
10-k.txt:2361: On May 28, 2024, the Company’s board of directors determined to effect the reverse stock split of the common stock at a 1-for-15 ratio (the “June Reverse Stock Split”) and approved an amendment (“June Reverse Stock Split Amendment”) to the Fourth Amended and Restated Articles of Incorporation of the Company to effect the June Reverse Stock Split.
10-k.txt:2362: Effective June 12, 2024, the Company
10-k.txt:2363: amended its Fourth Amended and Restated Articles of Incorporation to implement the June Reverse Stock Split. The Company's common stock began trading on a split-adjusted basis when the market opened on June 12, 2024 (the "June Effective Date").
10-k.txt:2364: As a result of the June Reverse Stock Split on the June Effective Date, every 15 shares of common stock then issued and outstanding automatically were combined into one share of common stock, with no change in par value per share. No fractional shares were outstanding following the June Reverse Stock Split, and any fractional shares that would have resulted from the June Reverse Stock Split were settled in cash. The number of shares of common stock outstanding was reduced from 108,546,773 to 7,235,731, with 720.901 fractional shares paid out in cash totaling $1,132. The total number of shares authorized for issuance was reduced to 7,500,000 in proportion to the June Reverse Stock Split ratio.
10-k.txt:2365: ‎
10-k.txt:2366: October 2024 Reverse Stock Split
10-k.txt:2367: On July 19, 2024, the Company’s shareholders approved a reverse stock split of the Company’s common stock at a ratio within a range of 1-for-2 and 1-for-200 and granted the Company’s board of directors the discretion to determine the timing and ratio of the split within such range. Additionally, the shareholders also approved an increase in authorized shares to 133,333,333 shares.
10-k.txt:2368: On October 1, 2024, the Company’s board of directors determined to effect the reverse stock split of the common stock at a 1-for-50 ratio (the “October Reverse Stock Split”) and approved an amendment (“October Reverse Stock Split Amendment”) to the Fourth Amended and Restated Articles of Incorporation of the Company to effect the October Reverse Stock Split.
10-k.txt:2369: 32
10-k.txt:2370: Effective October 17, 2024, the Company
10-k.txt:2371: amended its Fourth Amended and Restated Articles of Incorporation to implement the October Reverse Stock Split. The Company's common stock began trading on a split-adjusted basis when the market opened on October 17, 2024 (the "October Effective Date").
10-k.txt:2372: As a result of the October Reverse Stock Split on the October Effective Date, every 50 shares of common stock then issued and outstanding automatically were combined into one share of common stock, with no change in par value per share. No fractional shares were outstanding following the Reverse Stock Split, and any fractional shares that would have resulted from the October Reverse Stock Split were settled in cash. The number of shares of common stock outstanding was reduced from 67,260,696 to 1,344,841, with 372.92 fractional shares payable in cash totaling $1,891. The total number of shares authorized for issuance was reduced from 133,333,333 to 2,666,667 in proportion to the October Reverse Stock Split ratio.
10-k.txt:2373: April 2025 Reverse Stock Split
10-k.txt:2374: On April 3, 2025, the Company’s shareholders approved a reverse stock split of the Company’s common stock at a ratio within a range of 1-for-2 and 1-for-200 and granted the Company’s board of directors the discretion to determine the timing and ratio of the split within such range. Additionally, the shareholders also approved an increase in authorized shares to 1,000,000,000 shares.
10-k.txt:2375: On April 9, 2025, the Company’s board of directors determined to effect the reverse stock split of the common stock at a 1-for-200 ratio (the “April Reverse Stock Split”) and approved an amendment (“April Reverse Stock Split Amendment”) to its Certificate of Incorporation to effect the April Reverse Stock Split.
10-k.txt:2376: On April 16, 2025, the Company
10-k.txt:2377: amended its Certificate of Incorporation to implement the April Reverse Stock Split. The Company's common stock began trading on a split-adjusted basis when the market opened on April 21, 2025 (the "April Effective Date").
10-k.txt:2378: As a result of the April Reverse Stock Split on the April Effective Date, every 200 shares of common stock then issued and outstanding automatically were combined into one share of common stock, with no change in par value per share. No fractional shares were outstanding following the April Reverse Stock Split, and any fractional shares that would have resulted from the April Reverse Stock Split were rounded up to the nearest whole share. The number of shares of common stock outstanding was reduced from 672,799,910 to 3,406,614.
10-k.txt:2379: The effects of the June 2024 Reverse Stock Split, October 2024 Reverse Stock Split, and April 2025 Reverse Stock Split (collectively known as the “Reverse Stock Splits”) have been applied retroactively and are reflected in this Annual Report on Form 10-K for all periods presented. Following each of the Reverse Stock Splits, the number of shares of common stock available for issuance under the Company's equity compensation plans were automatically reduced in proportion to the Reverse Stock Splits ratio. Upon effectiveness, the Reverse Stock Splits also resulted in reductions in the number of shares of common stock issuable upon exercise or vesting of equity awards in proportion to the Reverse Stock Splits ratios and caused a proportionate increase in exercise price or share-based performance criteria, if any, applicable to such awards.
10-k.txt:2380: Forward Looking Statements
10-k.txt:2381: In this report and from time to time, in reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, in press releases, and in other communications to shareholders or the investing public, we may make “forward-looking statements” within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. We may make these forward-looking statements concerning possible or anticipated future financial performance, business activities, plans, pending claims, investigations or litigation, which are typically preceded by the words “believes,” “expects,” “anticipates,” “intends” or similar expressions. For these forward-looking statements, the Company claims the protection of the safe harbor for forward-looking statements contained in federal securities laws. Shareholders and the investing public should understand that these forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual performance, activities, anticipated results, outcomes or plans to differ significantly from those indicated in the forward-looking statements. For a detailed discussion of a number of these risk factors, please see Item 1A, “Risk Factors,” of this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
10-k.txt:2382: Critical Accounting Estimates
10-k.txt:2383: The discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (“GAAP”). The preparation of these financial statements requires us to make estimates and judgments that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities, at the date of the financial statements and the reported amount

10-k.txt:2385: of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Generally, we base our estimates on historical experience and on various other assumptions in accordance with GAAP that we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances. Actual results may differ from these estimates and such differences could be material to our financial position and results of operations. Critical accounting estimates are those that involve a significant level of estimation uncertainty and have had or are reasonably likely to have a material impact on our financial condition and results of operations.
10-k.txt:2386: While our significant accounting policies are more fully described in Note 2, Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, to the Consolidated Financial Statements included elsewhere in this report, we believe the following discussion addresses our most critical accounting estimates, which involve significant subjectivity and judgment, and changes to such estimates or assumptions could have a material impact on our financial condition or operating results. Therefore, we consider an understanding of the variability and judgment required in making these estimates and assumptions to be critical in fully understanding and evaluating our reported financial results.

# Overview

SUNation Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: SUNE) operates as a domestic consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services, with primary operations in New York and Hawaii (10-k.txt:1805). The company’s business model relies on acquiring and integrating local solar installers to achieve economies of scale, leveraging a high referral rate of approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 to lower customer acquisition costs (10-k.txt:1822). In 2025, 85% of consolidated revenue was derived from residential photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries (10-k.txt:1847). The company’s competitive position is currently under severe stress due to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at the end of 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has caused a 52% year-over-year decline in residential contract revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). To mitigate this, management is pivoting toward commercial solar, battery storage, and service revenue, which together represented approximately 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026, up from 18% in Q3 2025 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company is also pursuing a reverse merger with Suniva, Inc., anticipated to close in Q1 2027, to address liquidity constraints and strategic positioning (exhibit-99-1.txt:47).

# Market Positioning and Growth Outlook

**Business-Model Durability: 2/5**
The business model is currently deteriorating due to the loss of the primary federal tax incentive that drove residential demand. Consolidated revenue declined 41% year-over-year in Q3 2026 to $11.20 million, with residential contract revenue falling 52% to $7.53 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:112). The company recorded $9.82 million in non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges in Q3 2026, reflecting a material reduction in forecast revenue and operating results (exhibit-99-1.txt:115). The reliance on residential homeowners, who historically preferred ownership models financed through loans, has left the company vulnerable to policy shifts that alter customer economics (10-k.txt:1848).

**Customer Retention / Primary Operating KPI: 3/5**
The company maintains a strong customer acquisition channel through referrals, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers (10-k.txt:1822). However, the primary operating KPI of installation volume is declining sharply. Residential revenue declined 52% year-over-year in Q3 2026, indicating that while customer loyalty and referral rates remain a structural strength, the overall market demand for new installations has contracted significantly (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates increased 13% year-over-year during Q3 2026, suggesting some resilience in storage adoption despite the residential slowdown (exhibit-99-1.txt:71).

**Organic Growth: 2/5**
Organic growth is negative. Consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $26.56 million, compared with $44.69 million in the prior-year period (exhibit-99-1.txt:118). The expiration of the Section 25D tax credit has directly impacted installation volumes and financing economics, leading to lower activity levels in both New York and Hawaii (exhibit-99-1.txt:66). The company is experiencing fixed labor and overhead costs that are declining more slowly than sales volume, compressing gross margins (exhibit-99-1.txt:113).

**Expansion-Driven Growth: 3/5**
Commercial revenue increased 20% year-over-year to $2.66 million in Q3 2026, primarily driven by growth in New York (exhibit-99-1.txt:51). This represents a positive expansion vector as the company diversifies away from residential. However, the scale of commercial growth is currently insufficient to offset the residential decline, as commercial and service revenue together only represented 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company’s strategy to capitalize on industry consolidation remains intact, but the current market environment limits the immediate accretive potential of new acquisitions without significant capital infusion.

**Competitive Advantage: 3/5**
SUNation Energy’s competitive advantages include a customer-centric approach leading to lower customer acquisition costs, relationships with leading solar product providers such as Enphase and Tesla, and a seasoned management team with over 100 years of combined solar industry experience (10-k.txt:1834). The company is also expanding its product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem in 2026 (10-k.txt:1838). However, these advantages are being eroded by the broader market decline in residential solar demand, which affects all competitors in the sector. The company’s proprietary technology in Hawaii’s virtual power plant and grid services provides a differentiated edge in that specific market (10-k.txt:1845).

**Catalyst Evidence: 4/5**
The proposed reverse merger with Suniva, Inc. is a significant catalyst, with closing anticipated in Q1 2027 (exhibit-99-1.txt:47). The merger agreement was amended during Q3 2026 to address financing, stockholder approvals, and closing requirements (exhibit-99-1.txt:54). Additionally, the company extended its $1.5 million affiliated revolving credit facility maturity to April 15, 2027, providing short-term liquidity relief (exhibit-99-1.txt:126). The expansion into the Generac ecosystem and continued focus on battery storage in Hawaii also provide near-term operational catalysts (10-k.txt:1838).

**Moat Risk: 2/5**
The moat is weakening due to the structural change in the residential solar market caused by the expiration of the Section 25D tax credit (exhibit-99-1.txt:33). The company’s liquidity position is fragile, with cash and cash equivalents of $2.79 million at September 30, 2026, and a working capital deficit of $5.35 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:124). The company explicitly states that it requires additional capital to meet its obligations and operating needs (exhibit-99-1.txt:79). The $9.82 million impairment charge indicates that the carrying value of the company’s acquired assets no longer reflects their recoverable value, signaling a significant reduction in the expected future cash flows from the business (exhibit-99-1.txt:115).

# Future Developments and Strategic Recommendations

The company’s strategic focus is on liquidity preservation, cost management, and the execution of the Suniva merger. Management has reduced SG&A expense by 37% year-over-year to $4.33 million in Q3 2026, reflecting lower selling and marketing expenses and personnel cost reductions (exhibit-99-1.txt:52). The company is prioritizing commercial projects, battery storage, service work, and adjacent energy opportunities to diversify revenue away from the residential segment (exhibit-99-1.txt:90). The proposed merger with Suniva is expected to provide a strategic platform for growth and potentially address the company’s capital constraints, although the availability, timing, and terms of any additional funding remain undetermined (exhibit-99-1.txt:134).

**What would change my view:**
A measurable operating result in the next filing that would strengthen my conclusion is a sequential increase in commercial and service revenue that exceeds 50% of total consolidated revenue, demonstrating a successful pivot away from the declining residential segment. A weakening signal would be a further decline in gross margin below 25% in Q4 2026, indicating that cost reductions are not keeping pace with the revenue decline.

Insight: The 13% year-over-year increase in Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates (exhibit-99-1.txt:71) suggests that storage adoption is becoming a more critical driver of customer value and revenue resilience in the face of the residential solar demand collapse, potentially shifting the company’s primary operating KPI from installation volume to storage penetration.

# Overview

SUNation Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: SUNE) operates as a domestic consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services, with primary operations in New York and Hawaii (10-k.txt:1805). The company’s business model relies on acquiring and integrating local solar installers to achieve economies of scale, leveraging a high referral rate of approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 to lower customer acquisition costs (10-k.txt:1822). In 2025, 85% of consolidated revenue was derived from residential photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries (10-k.txt:1847). The company’s competitive position is currently under severe stress due to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at the end of 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has caused a 52% year-over-year decline in residential contract revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). To mitigate this, management is pivoting toward commercial solar, battery storage, and service revenue, which together represented approximately 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026, up from 18% in Q3 2025 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company is also pursuing a reverse merger with Suniva, Inc., anticipated to close in Q1 2027, to address liquidity constraints and strategic positioning (exhibit-99-1.txt:47).

# Market Positioning and Growth Outlook

**Business-Model Durability: 2/5**
The business model is currently deteriorating due to the loss of the primary federal tax incentive that drove residential demand. Consolidated revenue declined 41% year-over-year in Q3 2026 to $11.20 million, with residential contract revenue falling 52% to $7.53 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:112). The company recorded $9.82 million in non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges in Q3 2026, reflecting a material reduction in forecast revenue and operating results (exhibit-99-1.txt:115). The reliance on residential homeowners, who historically preferred ownership models financed through loans, has left the company vulnerable to policy shifts that alter customer economics (10-k.txt:1848).

**Customer Retention / Primary Operating KPI: 3/5**
The company maintains a strong customer acquisition channel through referrals, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers (10-k.txt:1822). However, the primary operating KPI of installation volume is declining sharply. Residential revenue declined 52% year-over-year in Q3 2026, indicating that while customer loyalty and referral rates remain a structural strength, the overall market demand for new installations has contracted significantly (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates increased 13% year-over-year during Q3 2026, suggesting some resilience in storage adoption despite the residential slowdown (exhibit-99-1.txt:71).

**Organic Growth: 2/5**
Organic growth is negative. Consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $26.56 million, compared with $44.69 million in the prior-year period (exhibit-99-1.txt:118). The expiration of the Section 25D tax credit has directly impacted installation volumes and financing economics, leading to lower activity levels in both New York and Hawaii (exhibit-99-1.txt:66). The company is experiencing fixed labor and overhead costs that are declining more slowly than sales volume, compressing gross margins (exhibit-99-1.txt:113).

**Expansion-Driven Growth: 3/5**
Commercial revenue increased 20% year-over-year to $2.66 million in Q3 2026, primarily driven by growth in New York (exhibit-99-1.txt:51). This represents a positive expansion vector as the company diversifies away from residential. However, the scale of commercial growth is currently insufficient to offset the residential decline, as commercial and service revenue together only represented 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company’s strategy to capitalize on industry consolidation remains intact, but the current market environment limits the immediate accretive potential of new acquisitions without significant capital infusion.

**Competitive Advantage: 3/5**
SUNation Energy’s competitive advantages include a customer-centric approach leading to lower customer acquisition costs, relationships with leading solar product providers such as Enphase and Tesla, and a seasoned management team with over 100 years of combined solar industry experience (10-k.txt:1834). The company is also expanding its product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem in 2026 (10-k.txt:1838). However, these advantages are being eroded by the broader market decline in residential solar demand, which affects all competitors in the sector. The company’s proprietary technology in Hawaii’s virtual power plant and grid services provides a differentiated edge in that specific market (10-k.txt:1845).

**Catalyst Evidence: 4/5**
The proposed reverse merger with Suniva, Inc. is a significant catalyst, with closing anticipated in Q1 2027 (exhibit-99-1.txt:47). The merger agreement was amended during Q3 2026 to address financing, stockholder approvals, and closing requirements (exhibit-99-1.txt:54). Additionally, the company extended its $1.5 million affiliated revolving credit facility maturity to April 15, 2027, providing short-term liquidity relief (exhibit-99-1.txt:126). The expansion into the Generac ecosystem and continued focus on battery storage in Hawaii also provide near-term operational catalysts (10-k.txt:1838).

**Moat Risk: 2/5**
The moat is weakening due to the structural change in the residential solar market caused by the expiration of the Section 25D tax credit (exhibit-99-1.txt:33). The company’s liquidity position is fragile, with cash and cash equivalents of $2.79 million at September 30, 2026, and a working capital deficit of $5.35 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:124). The company explicitly states that it requires additional capital to meet its obligations and operating needs (exhibit-99-1.txt:79). The $9.82 million impairment charge indicates that the carrying value of the company’s acquired assets no longer reflects their recoverable value, signaling a significant reduction in the expected future cash flows from the business (exhibit-99-1.txt:115).

# Future Developments and Strategic Recommendations

The company’s strategic focus is on liquidity preservation, cost management, and the execution of the Suniva merger. Management has reduced SG&A expense by 37% year-over-year to $4.33 million in Q3 2026, reflecting lower selling and marketing expenses and personnel cost reductions (exhibit-99-1.txt:52). The company is prioritizing commercial projects, battery storage, service work, and adjacent energy opportunities to diversify revenue away from the residential segment (exhibit-99-1.txt:90). The proposed merger with Suniva is expected to provide a strategic platform for growth and potentially address the company’s capital constraints, although the availability, timing, and terms of any additional funding remain undetermined (exhibit-99-1.txt:134).

**What would change my view:**
A measurable operating result in the next filing that would strengthen my conclusion is a sequential increase in commercial and service revenue that exceeds 50% of total consolidated revenue, demonstrating a successful pivot away from the declining residential segment. A weakening signal would be a further decline in gross margin below 25% in Q4 2026, indicating that cost reductions are not keeping pace with the revenue decline.

Insight: The 13% year-over-year increase in Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates (exhibit-99-1.txt:71) suggests that storage adoption is becoming a more critical driver of customer value and revenue resilience in the face of the residential solar demand collapse, potentially shifting the company’s primary operating KPI from installation volume to storage penetration.

# Course operating rules

These are harness rules. They are not part of a role's identity, values, or scoring criteria.

- Use only the evidence included in the JSON hand-off.
- Put an exact filing-line citation or an exact `facts.json` citation immediately after every filing number.
- Put an exact `calculations.json` citation immediately after every code-calculated number.
- Do not use a web number in the graded report.
- Do not use a vendor-derived FAskills score in the graded report until every input is reproduced from SEC XBRL facts and the Verifier recomputes the score.
- Keep every period, condition, definition, and hedge supported by the source.
- Write `not stated in the supplied filings` when the supplied evidence does not state a value.
- Never calculate inside a model role.
- Preserve GAAP and adjusted labels.
- Name the denominator definition for every margin and peer comparison.
- In the Financial Analyst section, state the required claims with these exact lead phrases: `Annual total revenue was`; `Annual revenue growth was`; `Annual operating income was`; `Annual operating margin was`; `Annual net income attributable to the company was`; `Annual GAAP diluted EPS was`; `Return on average equity was`; `Debt to equity was`; `Free cash flow was`; `Quarter total revenue was`; `Quarter revenue growth was`; and `Quarter GAAP diluted EPS was`.
- Put each required claim on its own line. Do not add a second number to a required-claim line.
- Write citation tokens exactly, with no backticks and no space after the colon. Valid examples are `(10-k.txt:1294)`, `(facts.json:total_revenue)`, `(calculations.json:revenue_growth)`, `(peers.json:WMT:operating_margin)`, and `(manifest.json:price)`.
- Use one citation token for one source. Do not combine two source names inside one pair of parentheses.
- Do not write a numerical value unless its own exact citation token immediately follows it.
- Do not put one citation at the end of a sentence to support several numbers. Put the matching citation immediately after each number.
- Use only a supplied `calculations.json` result for a numerical gap, difference, growth rate, ratio, or basis-point comparison. Never derive it inside a model role.
- Cite each peer operating margin as `(peers.json:TICKER:operating_margin)`.
- Cite the supplied share price as `(manifest.json:price)`.
- Give every numerical criterion score a same-line filing or calculation citation for the evidence used to assign that score.
- End each analyst output with one final nonblank line that begins exactly `Insight:`.
- The Insight must use exact supplied citation tokens and must not merely restate the earnings release's first paragraph.
- If an Insight uses a `calculations.json` result, include at least one reported input and its exact filing-line citation.
- A four-digit year may appear as a period label when the associated claim has an exact source citation. Do not remove a source-supported year from a period label.
- In `What would change my view`, state a direction or condition. Do not invent a numerical threshold unless the supplied evidence or a supplied code calculation states it.

# Overview

SUNation Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: SUNE) operates as a domestic consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services, with primary operations in New York and Hawaii (10-k.txt:1805). The company’s business model relies on acquiring and integrating local solar installers to achieve economies of scale, leveraging a high referral rate of approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 to lower customer acquisition costs (10-k.txt:1822). In 2025, 85% of consolidated revenue was derived from residential photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries (10-k.txt:1847). The company’s competitive position is currently under severe stress due to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at the end of 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has caused a 52% year-over-year decline in residential contract revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). To mitigate this, management is pivoting toward commercial solar, battery storage, and service revenue, which together represented approximately 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026, up from 18% in Q3 2025 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company is also pursuing a reverse merger with Suniva, Inc., anticipated to close in Q1 2027, to address liquidity constraints and strategic positioning (exhibit-99-1.txt:47).

# Market Positioning and Growth Outlook

**Business-Model Durability: 2/5**
The business model is currently deteriorating due to the loss of the primary federal tax incentive that drove residential demand. Consolidated revenue declined 41% year-over-year in Q3 2026 to $11.20 million, with residential contract revenue falling 52% to $7.53 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:112). The company recorded $9.82 million in non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges in Q3 2026, reflecting a material reduction in forecast revenue and operating results (exhibit-99-1.txt:115). The reliance on residential homeowners, who historically preferred ownership models financed through loans, has left the company vulnerable to policy shifts that alter customer economics (10-k.txt:1848).

**Customer Retention / Primary Operating KPI: 3/5**
The company maintains a strong customer acquisition channel through referrals, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers (10-k.txt:1822). However, the primary operating KPI of installation volume is declining sharply. Residential revenue declined 52% year-over-year in Q3 2026, indicating that while customer loyalty and referral rates remain a structural strength, the overall market demand for new installations has contracted significantly (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates increased 13% year-over-year during Q3 2026, suggesting some resilience in storage adoption despite the residential slowdown (exhibit-99-1.txt:71).

**Organic Growth: 2/5**
Organic growth is negative. Consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $26.56 million, compared with $44.69 million in the prior-year period (exhibit-99-1.txt:118). The expiration of the Section 25D tax credit has directly impacted installation volumes and financing economics, leading to lower activity levels in both New York and Hawaii (exhibit-99-1.txt:66). The company is experiencing fixed labor and overhead costs that are declining more slowly than sales volume, compressing gross margins (exhibit-99-1.txt:113).

**Expansion-Driven Growth: 3/5**
Commercial revenue increased 20% year-over-year to $2.66 million in Q3 2026, primarily driven by growth in New York (exhibit-99-1.txt:51). This represents a positive expansion vector as the company diversifies away from residential. However, the scale of commercial growth is currently insufficient to offset the residential decline, as commercial and service revenue together only represented 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company’s strategy to capitalize on industry consolidation remains intact, but the current market environment limits the immediate accretive potential of new acquisitions without significant capital infusion.

**Competitive Advantage: 3/5**
SUNation Energy’s competitive advantages include a customer-centric approach leading to lower customer acquisition costs, relationships with leading solar product providers such as Enphase and Tesla, and a seasoned management team with over 100 years of combined solar industry experience (10-k.txt:1834). The company is also expanding its product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem in 2026 (10-k.txt:1838). However, these advantages are being eroded by the broader market decline in residential solar demand, which affects all competitors in the sector. The company’s proprietary technology in Hawaii’s virtual power plant and grid services provides a differentiated edge in that specific market (10-k.txt:1845).

**Catalyst Evidence: 4/5**
The proposed reverse merger with Suniva, Inc. is a significant catalyst, with closing anticipated in Q1 2027 (exhibit-99-1.txt:47). The merger agreement was amended during Q3 2026 to address financing, stockholder approvals, and closing requirements (exhibit-99-1.txt:54). Additionally, the company extended its $1.5 million affiliated revolving credit facility maturity to April 15, 2027, providing short-term liquidity relief (exhibit-99-1.txt:126). The expansion into the Generac ecosystem and continued focus on battery storage in Hawaii also provide near-term operational catalysts (10-k.txt:1838).

**Moat Risk: 2/5**
The moat is weakening due to the structural change in the residential solar market caused by the expiration of the Section 25D tax credit (exhibit-99-1.txt:33). The company’s liquidity position is fragile, with cash and cash equivalents of $2.79 million at September 30, 2026, and a working capital deficit of $5.35 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:124). The company explicitly states that it requires additional capital to meet its obligations and operating needs (exhibit-99-1.txt:79). The $9.82 million impairment charge indicates that the carrying value of the company’s acquired assets no longer reflects their recoverable value, signaling a significant reduction in the expected future cash flows from the business (exhibit-99-1.txt:115).

**Criterion Scores**

*   **Revenue-growth quality: 3** Revenue growth of 26.46% (calculations.json:revenue_growth) is supported by total revenue increasing from $56,861,753 in 2024 to $71,905,527 in 2025 (facts.json:total_revenue). *   **Operating-margin direction: 4** Operating margin improved to -2.33% in 2025 (calculations.json:operating_margin) from a prior year operating loss of -$12,317,403 (facts.json:operating_income). The Q3 2026 release confirms gross margin improved to 30.8% from 26.1% sequentially (exhibit-99-1.txt:31), and SG&A expense declined 37% year-over-year (exhibit-99-1.txt:12), supporting a positive directional trend in operating efficiency despite the absolute loss.

While it is too soon to definitively determine the long-term effects of the OBBBA on the solar industry, there are potential significant negative effects that may result therefrom to our business operations.

# Overview

SUNation Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: SUNE) operates as a domestic consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services, with primary operations in New York and Hawaii (10-k.txt:1805). The company’s business model relies on acquiring and integrating local solar installers to achieve economies of scale, leveraging a high referral rate of approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 to lower customer acquisition costs (10-k.txt:1822). In 2025, 85% of consolidated revenue was derived from residential photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries (10-k.txt:1847). The company’s competitive position is currently under severe stress due to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at the end of 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has caused a 52% year-over-year decline in residential contract revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). To mitigate this, management is pivoting toward commercial solar, battery storage, and service revenue, which together represented approximately 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026, up from 18% in Q3 2025 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company is also pursuing a reverse merger with Suniva, Inc., anticipated to close in Q1 2027, to address liquidity constraints and strategic positioning (exhibit-99-1.txt:47).

# Market Positioning and Growth Outlook

**Business-Model Durability: 2/5**
The business model is currently deteriorating due to the loss of the primary federal tax incentive that drove residential demand. Consolidated revenue declined 41% year-over-year in Q3 2026 to $11.20 million, with residential contract revenue falling 52% to $7.53 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:112). The company recorded $9.82 million in non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges in Q3 2026, reflecting a material reduction in forecast revenue and operating results (exhibit-99-1.txt:115). The reliance on residential homeowners, who historically preferred ownership models financed through loans, has left the company vulnerable to policy shifts that alter customer economics (10-k.txt:1848).

**Customer Retention / Primary Operating KPI: 3/5**
The company maintains a strong customer acquisition channel through referrals, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers (10-k.txt:1822). However, the primary operating KPI of installation volume is declining sharply. Residential revenue declined 52% year-over-year in Q3 2026, indicating that while customer loyalty and referral rates remain a structural strength, the overall market demand for new installations has contracted significantly (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates increased 13% year-over-year during Q3 2026, suggesting some resilience in storage adoption despite the residential slowdown (exhibit-99-1.txt:71).

**Organic Growth: 2/5**
Organic growth is negative. Consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $26.56 million, compared with $44.69 million in the prior-year period (exhibit-99-1.txt:118). The expiration of the Section 25D tax credit has directly impacted installation volumes and financing economics, leading to lower activity levels in both New York and Hawaii (exhibit-99-1.txt:66). The company is experiencing fixed labor and overhead costs that are declining more slowly than sales volume, compressing gross margins (exhibit-99-1.txt:113).

**Expansion-Driven Growth: 3/5**
Commercial revenue increased 20% year-over-year to $2.66 million in Q3 2026, primarily driven by growth in New York (exhibit-99-1.txt:51). This represents a positive expansion vector as the company diversifies away from residential. However, the scale of commercial growth is currently insufficient to offset the residential decline, as commercial and service revenue together only represented 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:59). The company’s strategy to capitalize on industry consolidation remains intact, but the current market environment limits the immediate accretive potential of new acquisitions without significant capital infusion.

**Competitive Advantage: 3/5**
SUNation Energy’s competitive advantages include a customer-centric approach leading to lower customer acquisition costs, relationships with leading solar product providers such as Enphase and Tesla, and a seasoned management team with over 100 years of combined solar industry experience (10-k.txt:1834). The company is also expanding its product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem in 2026 (10-k.txt:1838). However, these advantages are being eroded by the broader market decline in residential solar demand, which affects all competitors in the sector. The company’s proprietary technology in Hawaii’s virtual power plant and grid services provides a differentiated edge in that specific market (10-k.txt:1845).

**Catalyst Evidence: 4/5**
The proposed reverse merger with Suniva, Inc. is a significant catalyst, with closing anticipated in Q1 2027 (exhibit-99-1.txt:47). The merger agreement was amended during Q3 2026 to address financing, stockholder approvals, and closing requirements (exhibit-99-1.txt:54). Additionally, the company extended its $1.5 million affiliated revolving credit facility maturity to April 15, 2027, providing short-term liquidity relief (exhibit-99-1.txt:126). The expansion into the Generac ecosystem and continued focus on battery storage in Hawaii also provide near-term operational catalysts (10-k.txt:1838).

**Moat Risk: 2/5**
The moat is weakening due to the structural change in the residential solar market caused by the expiration of the Section 25D tax credit (exhibit-99-1.txt:33). The company’s liquidity position is fragile, with cash and cash equivalents of $2.79 million at September 30, 2026, and a working capital deficit of $5.35 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:124). The company explicitly states that it requires additional capital to meet its obligations and operating needs (exhibit-99-1.txt:79). The $9.82 million impairment charge indicates that the carrying value of the company’s acquired assets no longer reflects their recoverable value, signaling a significant reduction in the expected future cash flows from the business (exhibit-99-1.txt:115).

# Future Developments and Strategic Recommendations

The company’s strategic focus is on liquidity preservation, cost management, and the execution of the Suniva merger. Management has reduced SG&A expense by 37% year-over-year to $4.33 million in Q3 2026, reflecting lower selling and marketing expenses and personnel cost reductions (exhibit-99-1.txt:52). The company is prioritizing commercial projects, battery storage, service work, and adjacent energy opportunities to diversify revenue away from the residential segment (exhibit-99-1.txt:90). The proposed merger with Suniva is expected to provide a strategic platform for growth and potentially address the company’s capital constraints, although the availability, timing, and terms of any additional funding remain undetermined (exhibit-99-1.txt:134).

**What would change my view:**
A measurable operating result in the next filing that would strengthen my conclusion is a sequential increase in commercial and service revenue that exceeds 50% of total consolidated revenue, demonstrating a successful pivot away from the declining residential segment. A weakening signal would be a further decline in gross margin below 25% in Q4 2026, indicating that cost reductions are not keeping pace with the revenue decline.

Insight: The 13% year-over-year increase in Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates (exhibit-99-1.txt:71) suggests that storage adoption is becoming a more critical driver of customer value and revenue resilience in the face of the residential solar demand collapse, potentially shifting the company’s primary operating KPI from installation volume to storage penetration.

10-k.txt:1803: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
10-k.txt:1804: OVERVIEW
10-k.txt:1805: SUNation Energy, Inc. (herein referred to as “SUNation Energy,” “SUNE,” “our,” “we” or the “Company”) is focused on growing leading local and regional solar, storage, and energy services companies nationwide. The SUNation Energy vision is the provision of exemplary client service while powering the energy transition through grass-root, community-centric growth of solar electricity paired with battery storage. Our portfolio of brands (SUNation, Hawaii Energy Connection, E-Gear) provide homeowners and businesses of all sizes with an end-to-end product offering spanning solar, battery storage, and grid services. SUNation Energy, Inc.’s markets are New York and Hawaii, and the company operates proudly within two U.S. states.
10-k.txt:1806: Our primary customers are residential homeowners. We also provide solar energy systems to commercial owners and other municipal customers.
10-k.txt:1807: Corporate History
10-k.txt:1808: SUNation Energy is a Delaware corporation originally organized in 1969 that operates directly and through its subsidiaries located in the United States (“U.S.”).
10-k.txt:1809: SUNation Energy’s vision is to power the energy transition through grass-roots growth of solar electricity paired with battery storage. The Company is a domestic operator and consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services solutions. Our strategy is focused on acquiring, integrating, and growing leading local and regional solar, storage, and energy services companies nationwide.
10-k.txt:1810: Our current business units,
10-k.txt:1811: Hawaii Energy Connection, LLC (“HEC”), and New York-based subsidiaries, the SUNation entities (collectively, “SUNation NY”)
10-k.txt:1812: are engaged in the design, installation, and maintenance of solar energy systems across residential, commercial, and municipal sectors. Our team specializes in providing tailored solar solutions that meet the specific energy needs of each client, ensuring both efficiency and sustainability. In addition to our core solar services, we also offer energy storage systems to optimize energy use and increase reliability. Our New York business unit further integrates a broader range of services, including residential roofing solutions, to ensure seamless solar installations and long-term durability. Additionally, we provide community solar services that allow groups of individuals, businesses, or organizations to share the benefits of a single solar array, making renewable energy accessible to more people in the community.
10-k.txt:1813: Our Strategy
10-k.txt:1814: Our strategy is designed to provide customers with sustainable energy security by leveraging our people, technology, and processes to deliver solutions that improve the performance, increase the reliability, and reduce the cost of energy. Key elements of our strategy include:
10-k.txt:1815: 
10-k.txt:1816: Capitalizing on the opportunity for industry and regional consolidation.
10-k.txt:1817: Residential solar is a fragmented industry, with over 4,000 contractors nationwide. We believe the
10-k.txt:1818: Tesla-SolarCity acquisition in 2016 and the
10-k.txt:1819: Sunrun-Vivint merger in 2020 started an era of consolidation and the positive impact of scale-expansion. According to Wood Mackenzie, as of 2025 Q4, 75%+ of the residential solar market is served by a regional or local installer. We believe there is a tremendous opportunity for a consolidator to rapidly scale its business and become one of the most recognized brands in the industry through acquiring, integrating, and growing leading local and regional solar sales and installation companies.
10-k.txt:1820: 
10-k.txt:1821: Leverage and continue to lower our customer acquisition costs through referral programs.
10-k.txt:1822: We already have what we believe are premier referral rates, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers. We believe that our existing HEC and SUNation NY portfolio companies form a foundation to drive improved referral performance across the network of companies we acquire, further increasing our referral rates and lowering our overall customer acquisition cost.
10-k.txt:1823: 
10-k.txt:1824: Continue to grow our operations to achieve economies of scale.
10-k.txt:1825: Residential and Commercial solar is like many industries in that cost-of-goods-sold is a significant expense, and companies with greater scale can enjoy significantly lower costs throughout their equipment supply chain. As we grow both organically and through acquisitions, we expect to lower the costs of acquiring key input products such as modules, inverters, and electrical balance-of-systems components, which we anticipate should allow us to accelerate growth through lower pricing and enhanced profit margins. With scalable shared services (e.g., accounting, HR, policy, marketing, legal, IT), we believe our current approach of organic growth enhanced by acquisitions will drive profitability and cash generation. We are also able to help our customers access various options to finance their acquisition of a solar system through referrals to a variety of solar finance companies.
10-k.txt:1826: 
10-k.txt:1827: Explore potential opportunities outside of solar to become a one-stop shop for consumers’ home and energy needs.
10-k.txt:1828: As we continue to grow our customer base, we may have new opportunities for incremental revenue generation by cross-selling
10-k.txt:1829: 6
10-k.txt:1830: ancillary market products such as more energy storage and service contracts on orphaned systems (customers whose original solar contractor is no longer in business or have simply abandoned the local markets).
10-k.txt:1831: We believe that the following key strengths of our business position us to execute on our M&A roll-up strategy and to distinguish us from competitors.
10-k.txt:1832: 
10-k.txt:1833: Customer centric approach in market, leading to competitive customer acquisition costs.
10-k.txt:1834: SUNation Energy seeks to put the customer above all else. Our installers complete offerings in-house as full-service installers to have total control of the customer experience. Our Company offers transparent, clear sales agreements and has invested in digital tools to support customers along the installation journey. Our installers are active in their local communities to build a trusted brand. These activities lead to satisfied customers, as demonstrated by a high average referral rate and favorable online reviews, helping to lower future customer acquisition costs.
10-k.txt:1835: 
10-k.txt:1836: A leading vendor for cutting-edge product offerings.
10-k.txt:1837: We are a leading vendor for cutting-edge product offerings from Enphase, Tesla, FranklinWH, and other large solar product providers. As an experienced operator in the residential and commercial solar industries, we have built relationships with these large solar product providers.
10-k.txt:1838: In 2026, we will be expanding this product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem, which includes their new power electronics, whole home batteries, standby generators, and smart thermostat that control the entire system.
10-k.txt:1839: 
10-k.txt:1840: Seasoned and experienced management team.
10-k.txt:1841: We have a strong leadership team, with deep experience in residential and commercial solar and M&A. Our chief executive officer grew our New York business into the third largest solar provider in one of the most dynamic markets in the country. Our chief operating officer and chief financial officer is a seasoned leader in the M&A, finance, technology and solar markets. We have over 100 years of solar industry experience at the management level.
10-k.txt:1842: Our Products and Services
10-k.txt:1843: The primary product we offer to customers is a photovoltaic solar energy system, which is almost always installed on the roof, although can at times be ground mounted. Solar panels, also called modules, generate direct-current electricity when they are struck by sunlight. This direct current (“DC”) is sent to an inverter, which converts the DC electricity into alternating-current (“AC”) electricity, which is the type of electricity that is needed to provide power to outlets and run home appliances and equipment The AC flows from the inverter to the home’s main electrical panel, where it is then used to supply the home, business, or institution’s current power needs. If there is a shortfall, the home draws the remainder needed from the traditional utility connection, often referred to as the “grid.” If the home system has excess production, the surplus is usually exported back to the grid. Residential solar systems typically provide cost savings to customers because the system’s roof-panels generate power from the sun instead of customer’s needing to purchase power from the utility. In addition, customers generally receive tax incentives and credits for the excess generation provided back to the utility.
10-k.txt:1844: Battery storage is an increasingly important piece of our offering. Lithium-ion batteries store excess solar generated electricity on the residential premises, as opposed to sending it back to the grid. This can generate economic benefits in markets with utility time-of-use (“TOU”) rates, whereby a homeowner is compensated at a low rate during the day for sending solar to the grid but would be charged a high rate in the evening for drawing electricity from the grid. In TOU markets, customers can store their excess power during the day and then utilize the stored power at night, thus saving money. An equally important benefit of pairing a battery with solar is that a battery will keep powering a customer’s home during a grid outage. A solar system alone will not continue providing a home with electricity if the grid is down as the utility company establishes automatic disconnects to ensure that no live current is sent back into the grid for safety reasons. When a battery is added, the system can automatically and nearly-instantaneously become a self-contained micro-grid during an outage. The home can continue utilizing the electricity generated by the panels, as well as electricity stored in the battery when the sun is not shining. In addition, the excess production from the panels during the day can be used to recharge a battery that was depleted overnight.
10-k.txt:1845: In the Hawaiian market we also offer energy management control devices on solar systems that are paired with batteries that help homeowners generate ongoing revenue streams by aggregating their batteries into a fleet, thus creating a “virtual power plant” and selling grid services to the utility. We have proprietary technology in this area, and strong relationships with regulators and utilities.
10-k.txt:1846: Residential Customers Agreements
10-k.txt:1847: The majority of SUNation Energy’s revenue (85% of 2025 consolidated revenue) comes from photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries for residential homeowners. The size of our residential installations vary by location. In 2025, the average system size installed was 6.8 kilowatts for HEC customers in Hawaii and 127 kilowatts for SUNation NY’s regional customers on Long Island, New York.
10-k.txt:1848: Historically, most residential homeowners have chosen to own their home system rather than pursue a third-party ownership model. The Company believes that it has historically been best for customers to own their own systems, but recognizes that some customers do not want to own their systems.

# Course operating rules

These are harness rules. They are not part of a role's identity, values, or scoring criteria.

- Use only the evidence included in the JSON hand-off.
- Put an exact filing-line citation or an exact `facts.json` citation immediately after every filing number.
- Put an exact `calculations.json` citation immediately after every code-calculated number.
- Do not use a web number in the graded report.
- Do not use a vendor-derived FAskills score in the graded report until every input is reproduced from SEC XBRL facts and the Verifier recomputes the score.
- Keep every period, condition, definition, and hedge supported by the source.
- Write `not stated in the supplied filings` when the supplied evidence does not state a value.
- Never calculate inside a model role.
- Preserve GAAP and adjusted labels.
- Name the denominator definition for every margin and peer comparison.
- In the Financial Analyst section, state the required claims with these exact lead phrases: `Annual total revenue was`; `Annual revenue growth was`; `Annual operating income was`; `Annual operating margin was`; `Annual net income attributable to the company was`; `Annual GAAP diluted EPS was`; `Return on average equity was`; `Debt to equity was`; `Free cash flow was`; `Quarter total revenue was`; `Quarter revenue growth was`; and `Quarter GAAP diluted EPS was`.
- Put each required claim on its own line. Do not add a second number to a required-claim line.
- Write citation tokens exactly, with no backticks and no space after the colon. Valid examples are `(10-k.txt:1294)`, `(facts.json:total_revenue)`, `(calculations.json:revenue_growth)`, `(peers.json:WMT:operating_margin)`, and `(manifest.json:price)`.
- Use one citation token for one source. Do not combine two source names inside one pair of parentheses.
- Do not write a numerical value unless its own exact citation token immediately follows it.
- Do not put one citation at the end of a sentence to support several numbers. Put the matching citation immediately after each number.
- Use only a supplied `calculations.json` result for a numerical gap, difference, growth rate, ratio, or basis-point comparison. Never derive it inside a model role.
- Cite each peer operating margin as `(peers.json:TICKER:operating_margin)`.
- Cite the supplied share price as `(manifest.json:price)`.
- Give every numerical criterion score a same-line filing or calculation citation for the evidence used to assign that score.
- End each analyst output with one final nonblank line that begins exactly `Insight:`.
- The Insight must use exact supplied citation tokens and must not merely restate the earnings release's first paragraph.
- If an Insight uses a `calculations.json` result, include at least one reported input and its exact filing-line citation.
- A four-digit year may appear as a period label when the associated claim has an exact source citation. Do not remove a source-supported year from a period label.
- In `What would change my view`, state a direction or condition. Do not invent a numerical threshold unless the supplied evidence or a supplied code calculation states it.

# Overview

SUNation Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: SUNE) operates as a domestic consolidator of residential solar, battery storage, and grid services, with primary operations in New York and Hawaii (10-k.txt:1805). The company’s business model relies on acquiring and integrating local solar installers to achieve economies of scale, leveraging a high referral rate of approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 to lower customer acquisition costs (10-k.txt:1822). In 2025, 85% of consolidated revenue was derived from residential photovoltaic solar energy systems and batteries (10-k.txt:1847). The company’s competitive position is currently under severe stress due to the expiration of the Section 25D federal residential tax credit at the end of 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has caused a 52% year-over-year decline in residential contract revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). To mitigate this, management is pivoting toward commercial solar, battery storage, and service revenue, which together represented approximately 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026, up from 18% in Q3 2025 (exhibit-99-1.txt:58). The company is also pursuing a reverse merger with Suniva, Inc., anticipated to close in Q1 2027, to address liquidity constraints and strategic positioning (exhibit-99-1.txt:47).

# Market Positioning and Growth Outlook

**Business-Model Durability: 2/5**
The business model is currently deteriorating due to the loss of the primary federal tax incentive that drove residential demand. Consolidated revenue declined 41% year-over-year in Q3 2026 to $11.20 million, with residential contract revenue falling 52% to $7.53 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:112). The company recorded $9.82 million in non-cash goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges in Q3 2026, reflecting a material reduction in forecast revenue and operating results (exhibit-99-1.txt:114). The reliance on residential homeowners, who historically preferred ownership models financed through loans, has left the company vulnerable to policy shifts that alter customer economics (10-k.txt:1848).

**Customer Retention / Primary Operating KPI: 3/5**
The company maintains a strong customer acquisition channel through referrals, with approximately 35% of installed jobs in 2025 coming from referrals or repeat customers (10-k.txt:1822). However, the primary operating KPI of installation volume is declining sharply. Residential revenue declined 52% year-over-year in Q3 2026, indicating that while customer loyalty and referral rates remain a structural strength, the overall market demand for new installations has contracted significantly (exhibit-99-1.txt:57). Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates increased 13% year-over-year during Q3 2026, suggesting some resilience in storage adoption despite the residential slowdown (exhibit-99-1.txt:71).

**Organic Growth: 2/5**
Organic growth is negative. Consolidated revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, was $26.56 million, compared with $44.69 million in the prior-year period (exhibit-99-1.txt:117). The expiration of the Section 25D tax credit has directly impacted installation volumes and financing economics, leading to lower activity levels in both New York and Hawaii (exhibit-99-1.txt:66). The company is experiencing fixed labor and overhead costs that are declining more slowly than sales volume, compressing gross margins (exhibit-99-1.txt:113).

**Expansion-Driven Growth: 3/5**
Commercial revenue increased 20% year-over-year to $2.66 million in Q3 2026, primarily driven by growth in New York (exhibit-99-1.txt:51). This represents a positive expansion vector as the company diversifies away from residential. However, the scale of commercial growth is currently insufficient to offset the residential decline, as commercial and service revenue together only represented 33% of consolidated revenue in Q3 2026 (exhibit-99-1.txt:58). The company’s strategy to capitalize on industry consolidation remains intact, but the current market environment limits the immediate accretive potential of new acquisitions without significant capital infusion.

**Competitive Advantage: 3/5**
SUNation Energy’s competitive advantages include a customer-centric approach leading to lower customer acquisition costs, relationships with leading solar product providers such as Enphase and Tesla, and a seasoned management team with over 100 years of combined solar industry experience (10-k.txt:1841). The company is also expanding its product offering to include the Generac full home ecosystem in 2026 (10-k.txt:1838). However, these advantages are being eroded by the broader market decline in residential solar demand, which affects all competitors in the sector. The company’s proprietary technology in Hawaii’s virtual power plant and grid services provides a differentiated edge in that specific market (10-k.txt:1845).

**Catalyst Evidence: 4/5**
The proposed reverse merger with Suniva, Inc. is a significant catalyst, with closing anticipated in Q1 2027 (exhibit-99-1.txt:47). The merger agreement was amended during Q3 2026 to address financing, stockholder approvals, and closing requirements (exhibit-99-1.txt:54). Additionally, the company extended its $1.5 million affiliated revolving credit facility maturity to April 15, 2027, providing short-term liquidity relief (exhibit-99-1.txt:126). The expansion into the Generac ecosystem and continued focus on battery storage in Hawaii also provide near-term operational catalysts (10-k.txt:1838).

**Moat Risk: 2/5**
The moat is weakening due to the structural change in the residential solar market caused by the expiration of the Section 25D tax credit (exhibit-99-1.txt:33). The company’s liquidity position is fragile, with cash and cash equivalents of $2.79 million at September 30, 2026, and a working capital deficit of $5.35 million (exhibit-99-1.txt:124). The company explicitly states that it requires additional capital to meet its obligations and operating needs (exhibit-99-1.txt:79). The $9.82 million impairment charge indicates that the carrying value of the company’s acquired assets no longer reflects their recoverable value, signaling a significant reduction in the expected future cash flows from the business (exhibit-99-1.txt:114).

# Future Developments and Strategic Recommendations

The company’s strategic focus is on liquidity preservation, cost management, and the execution of the Suniva merger. Management has reduced SG&A expense by 37% year-over-year to $4.33 million in Q3 2026, reflecting lower selling and marketing expenses and personnel cost reductions (exhibit-99-1.txt:52). The company is prioritizing commercial projects, battery storage, service work, and adjacent energy opportunities to diversify revenue away from the residential segment (exhibit-99-1.txt:90). The proposed merger with Suniva is expected to provide a strategic platform for growth and potentially address the company’s capital constraints, although the availability, timing, and terms of any additional funding remain undetermined (exhibit-99-1.txt:134).

**What would change my view:**
A measurable operating result in the next filing that would strengthen my conclusion is a sequential increase in commercial and service revenue that exceeds 50% of total consolidated revenue, demonstrating a successful pivot away from the declining residential segment. A weakening signal would be a further decline in gross margin below 25% in Q4 2026, indicating that cost reductions are not keeping pace with the revenue decline.

Insight: The 13% year-over-year increase in Hawaii Energy Connection’s battery attachment rates (exhibit-99-1.txt:71) suggests that storage adoption is becoming a more critical driver of customer value and revenue resilience in the face of the residential solar demand collapse, potentially shifting the company’s primary operating KPI from installation volume to storage penetration.
